section: Part A1 - Performance, Recovery and Injury Prevention
flagRule: Primary flag when the correct option is more than 8 characters longer than the median of the three distractors or when total option-length spread exceeds 15 characters.

originalOptions: Add accessory volume to create a final stimulus
Reduce volume while retaining selected quality lifts
Repeat maximum tests to confirm readiness
Stop resistance training before the final
revisedOptions: Add accessory volume before the final
Reduce volume; retain quality lifts
Repeat maximal tests before the final
Stop lifting until competition
changedQuestions.reviewerNote: Shortened the taper alternatives into comparable action phrases. The keyed plan still reduces volume while retaining a quality lifting stimulus, consistent with tapering and strength-conditioning principles; no filler wording was added.

originalOptions: Use the uninjured limb’s best jump as the only target
Count weeks since surgery rather than function
Begin maximal depth jumps at the next session
Progress power using force, symptoms, and landing quality
revisedOptions: Use the other limb as the only target
Progress by calendar time alone
Start maximal depth jumps immediately
Use force, symptoms, and landing quality
changedQuestions.reviewerNote: Converted the four choices to concise, parallel progression decisions. The keyed option preserves force, symptoms, and landing-quality criteria for power progression, while the distractors remain plausible but clinically insufficient alternatives.

originalOptions: Assume unchanged load is automatically safe
Consider maturation, tolerance, recovery, and symptoms
Increase intensity to overcome temporary soreness
Compare the athlete only with adult standards
revisedOptions: Assume unchanged load is automatically safe
Consider maturation, tolerance, recovery, symptoms
Increase intensity despite rising soreness
Compare readiness with adult standards alone
changedQuestions.reviewerNote: Kept the maturation and recovery concepts required by the load-management source, while making the alternatives parallel and clinically meaningful: unchanged-load assumptions, escalation despite symptoms, and adult-only comparison.

originalOptions: Increase volume while preserving usual fatigue
Reduce volume while monitoring performance and recovery
Use mood alone and ignore training records
Remove all training without considering response
revisedOptions: Increase volume and preserve accumulated fatigue
Reduce volume; monitor readiness and recovery
Use mood alone to set training volume
Stop all training without checking response
changedQuestions.reviewerNote: Recast the taper choices as parallel load-management actions. The keyed option retains reduction of volume with monitoring of readiness and recovery; the alternatives represent excessive loading, single-source monitoring, or unnecessary cessation.

originalOptions: Gentle mobility and low-intensity aerobic movement
Repeated sprints at competition intensity
A long circuit taken to technical failure
Heavy eccentric training for the most fatigued muscles
revisedOptions: Gentle mobility with easy aerobic work
Repeated sprints at competition intensity
A circuit continued to technical failure
Heavy eccentric work for fatigued muscles
changedQuestions.reviewerNote: Preserved low-intensity mobility and aerobic movement as the active-recovery prescription, while shortening redundant wording in all options. The distractors still represent progressively demanding work that could add load during a congested week.

originalOptions: Increase competition volume to adapt under fatigue quickly
Use age-appropriate technique, landing, and strength work
Exclude the athlete until growth is complete
Apply an adult programme without modification
revisedOptions: Increase competition volume despite growth changes
Use age-appropriate technique, landing, and strength
Exclude the athlete until growth changes settle
Apply an adult programme without developmental changes
changedQuestions.reviewerNote: Retained the developmentally appropriate prevention plan covering technique, landing, and strength. The distractors now express distinct unsafe choices—greater exposure, exclusion, and unmodified adult programming—in comparable language.

originalOptions: Clear the athlete because the screen is normal
Repeat the screen until the pain disappears
Allow play if the athlete completes warm-up
Use the symptom report to prompt clinical assessment
revisedOptions: Clear the athlete because screening was normal
Repeat screening until the pain disappears
Allow play after a symptom-free warm-up
Refer new sharp pain for clinical assessment
changedQuestions.reviewerNote: Preserved the clinical-safety meaning that new sharp pain warrants assessment despite a normal screen. The alternatives remain plausible screening errors and were brought into parallel decision wording.
